claim: Slc30a1 plays an essential role in maintaining cellular zinc homeostasis.
source: The zinc transporter Slc30a1 plays an essential role in maintaining cellular zinc homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about Slc30a1's function.

claim: The functional role of Slc30a1 in macrophages remains largely unknown.
source: Despite this, its functional role in macrophages remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: Bulk transcriptome sequencing in primary macrophages identifies Slc30a1 as a candidate in response to Salmonella infection.
source: Bulk transcriptome sequencing in primary macrophages identifies Slc30a1 as a candidate in response to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slc30a1 expression is increased in infected macrophages with localization at the plasma membrane and in the cytosol.
source: Whole-mount immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy imaging of primary macrophage and spleen from Salmonella-infected Slc30a1flag-EGFP mice demonstrate Slc30a1 expression is increased in infected macrophages with localization at the plasma membrane and in the cytosol.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and microscopy data from the reporter mice.

claim: Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice exhibit increased susceptibility to Salmonella infection compared to control littermates.
source: Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice (Slc30a1fl/fl;Lyz2-Cre) exhibit increased susceptibility to Salmonella infection compared to control littermates.
evidence: This is supported by survival data and bacterial burden measurements in the conditional knockout mice.

claim: Slc30a1-deficient macrophages are defective in intracellular killing.
source: We demonstrate that Slc30a1-deficient macrophages are defective in intracellular killing, which correlated with reduced activation of nuclear factor kappa B and reduction in nitric oxide (NO) production.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial killing assays and measurements of NF-κB activation and NO production.

claim: Slc30a1-deficient macrophages show reduced activation of nuclear factor kappa B.
source: We demonstrate that Slc30a1-deficient macrophages are defective in intracellular killing, which correlated with reduced activation of nuclear factor kappa B and reduction in nitric oxide (NO) production.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis of p-p65 and related signaling molecules.

claim: Slc30a1-deficient macrophages show reduction in nitric oxide (NO) production.
source: We demonstrate that Slc30a1-deficient macrophages are defective in intracellular killing, which correlated with reduced activation of nuclear factor kappa B and reduction in nitric oxide (NO) production.
evidence: This is supported by nitrite concentration measurements and iNOS protein levels.

claim: Slc30a1-deficient macrophages exhibit intracellular zinc accumulation.
source: Notably, the model exhibits intracellular zinc accumulation, demonstrating that Slc30a1 is required for zinc export.
evidence: This is supported by FluoZin-3 fluorescence measurements showing higher intracellular zinc in Slc30a1 cKO cells.

claim: Slc30a1 is required for zinc export.
source: Notably, the model exhibits intracellular zinc accumulation, demonstrating that Slc30a1 is required for zinc export.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of Slc30a1 leads to intracellular zinc accumulation.

claim: Zinc export enables the efficient NO-mediated antibacterial activity of macrophages to control invading Salmonella.
source: We thus conclude that zinc export enables the efficient NO-mediated antibacterial activity of macrophages to control invading Salmonella.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined observations of zinc accumulation, reduced NO production, and impaired bacterial killing in Slc30a1-deficient macrophages.

claim: Salmonella infection is one of the leading causes of diarrhea-related death, particularly among children under 5 years of age.
source: According to the 2015 Global Burden of Disease Study, Salmonella infection is one of the leading causes of diarrhea-related death, particularly among children under 5 years of age (Troeger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the 2015 Global Burden of Disease Study.

claim: Severe cases of Salmonella septicemia are associated with a 25% mortality rate.
source: Severe cases of Salmonella septicemia are associated with a 25% mortality rate (Feasey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feasey et al., 2012.

claim: Zinc deficiency has been linked to the incidence of Salmonella infection.
source: Based on epidemiological reports, zinc deficiency has been linked to the incidence of Salmonella infection (Troeger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to epidemiological reports.

claim: Zinc is involved in a wide range of fundamental biological processes, including modulating the immune system's response to invading pathogens.
source: As an essential micronutrient, zinc is involved in a wide range of fundamental biological processes, including modulating the immune system's response to invading pathogens (Wessels et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wessels et al., 2021.

claim: Zinc homeostasis is tightly regulated by two families of zinc transporters: Slc30a (ZnTs) and Slc39a (ZIPs).
source: In mammalian cells, zinc homeostasis is tightly regulated by two families of zinc transporters, namely solute carrier family 30 (Slc30a, also known as ZnTs) and solute carrier family 39 (Slc39a, also known as ZIPs), which export and import cellular zinc, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc transporter families.

claim: Slc30a family transporters export cellular zinc.
source: In mammalian cells, zinc homeostasis is tightly regulated by two families of zinc transporters, namely solute carrier family 30 (Slc30a, also known as ZnTs) and solute carrier family 39 (Slc39a, also known as ZIPs), which export and import cellular zinc, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Slc30a transporters.

claim: Slc39a family transporters import cellular zinc.
source: In mammalian cells, zinc homeostasis is tightly regulated by two families of zinc transporters, namely solute carrier family 30 (Slc30a, also known as ZnTs) and solute carrier family 39 (Slc39a, also known as ZIPs), which export and import cellular zinc, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Slc39a transporters.

claim: Zinc imbalance caused by the dysfunction of zinc transporters contributes to impaired hematopoiesis and macrophage survival.
source: Zinc imbalance caused by the dysfunction of zinc transporters contributes to impaired hematopoiesis and macrophage survival (He et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2023 and Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Slc30a1 (ZnT1) is ubiquitously expressed in mammalian cells.
source: Slc30a1 (ZnT1) is ubiquitously expressed in mammalian cells and is localized primarily at the plasma membrane (Nishito and Kambe, 2019; Golan et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2010), where it enables the export of cytoplasmic zinc to the extracellular space (Shusterman et al., 2017; Kambe et al., 2015; Kimura and Kambe, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishito and Kambe, 2019; Golan et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2010.

claim: Slc30a1 is localized primarily at the plasma membrane.
source: Slc30a1 (ZnT1) is ubiquitously expressed in mammalian cells and is localized primarily at the plasma membrane (Nishito and Kambe, 2019; Golan et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2010), where it enables the export of cytoplasmic zinc to the extracellular space (Shusterman et al., 2017; Kambe et al., 2015; Kimura and Kambe, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishito and Kambe, 2019; Golan et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2010.

claim: Slc30a1 enables the export of cytoplasmic zinc to the extracellular space.
source: Slc30a1 (ZnT1) is ubiquitously expressed in mammalian cells and is localized primarily at the plasma membrane (Nishito and Kambe, 2019; Golan et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2010), where it enables the export of cytoplasmic zinc to the extracellular space (Shusterman et al., 2017; Kambe et al., 2015; Kimura and Kambe, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shusterman et al., 2017; Kambe et al., 2015; Kimura and Kambe, 2016.

claim: Loss of Slc30a1 causes early embryonic death in mice.
source: In mice, loss of Slc30a1 causes early embryonic death (Andrews et al., 2004), suggesting that Slc30a1 is essential for early development and survival.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andrews et al., 2004.

claim: Slc30a1 is essential for early development and survival.
source: In mice, loss of Slc30a1 causes early embryonic death (Andrews et al., 2004), suggesting that Slc30a1 is essential for early development and survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of Slc30a1 causes early embryonic death.

claim: Slc30a1 expression is induced by a wide range of pathogens, including bacteria.
source: Recent data provide evidence that Slc30a1 expression is induced by a wide range of pathogens, including bacteria (Botella et al., 2011; Stocks et al., 2021), fungi (Rossi et al., 2021), and viruses (Moskovskich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Botella et al., 2011 and Stocks et al., 2021.

claim: Slc30a1 expression is induced by fungi.
source: Recent data provide evidence that Slc30a1 expression is induced by a wide range of pathogens, including bacteria (Botella et al., 2011; Stocks et al., 2021), fungi (Rossi et al., 2021), and viruses (Moskovskich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rossi et al., 2021.

claim: Slc30a1 expression is induced by viruses.
source: Recent data provide evidence that Slc30a1 expression is induced by a wide range of pathogens, including bacteria (Botella et al., 2011; Stocks et al., 2021), fungi (Rossi et al., 2021), and viruses (Moskovskich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moskovskich et al., 2019.

claim: Macrophages serve as the front line in the innate immune system by detecting and eliminating foreign pathogens.
source: Macrophages serve as the front line in the innate immune system by detecting and eliminating foreign pathogens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of macrophages in immunity.

claim: When Salmonella invades tissues, the bacteria are rapidly engulfed and killed by resident macrophages.
source: When Salmonella invades tissues, the bacteria are rapidly engulfed and killed by resident macrophages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the macrophage response to Salmonella.

claim: Rapid engulfment and killing of Salmonella by macrophages result in bacterial clearance, cytokine production, and the recruitment of polymorphonuclear phagocytes.
source: This rapid engulfment and killing of Salmonella by macrophages result in bacterial clearance, cytokine production, and the recruitment of polymorphonuclear phagocytes (Mastroeni et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mastroeni et al., 2009.

claim: RNA sequencing revealed a total of 1074 differentially expressed genes in Salmonella-infected BMDMs compared to control-treated BMDMs.
source: Our analysis revealed a total of 1074 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), defined as an absolute log2 fold change >1 and an adjusted p value of <0.05 compared to control-treated BMDMs (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Significantly downregulated genes in Salmonella-infected BMDMs were enriched in anti-inflammatory pathways, including Gpx1, Smad7, and Tgfb3.
source: Among these 1074 genes, significantly downregulated genes were enriched in anti-inflammatory pathways, including Gpx1, Smad7, and Tgfb3, and significantly upregulated genes were enriched in infectious and inflammatory pathways, including Tnf, Il6, Il1β, Ptgs2, and Nos2, suggesting a potent antimicrobial response in infected macrophages (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and pathway analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Significantly upregulated genes in Salmonella-infected BMDMs were enriched in infectious and inflammatory pathways, including Tnf, Il6, Il1β, Ptgs2, and Nos2.
source: Among these 1074 genes, significantly downregulated genes were enriched in anti-inflammatory pathways, including Gpx1, Smad7, and Tgfb3, and significantly upregulated genes were enriched in infectious and inflammatory pathways, including Tnf, Il6, Il1β, Ptgs2, and Nos2, suggesting a potent antimicrobial response in infected macrophages (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and pathway analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Gene expression patterns in Salmonella-infected BMDMs suggest a potent antimicrobial response.
source: Among these 1074 genes, significantly downregulated genes were enriched in anti-inflammatory pathways, including Gpx1, Smad7, and Tgfb3, and significantly upregulated genes were enriched in infectious and inflammatory pathways, including Tnf, Il6, Il1β, Ptgs2, and Nos2, suggesting a potent antimicrobial response in infected macrophages (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of gene expression changes observed in the RNA-seq data.

claim: KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of DEGs yielded 54 pathways (p < 0.05) involved largely in infectious diseases.
source: while Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis of these DEGs yielded 54 pathways (p < 0.05) involved largely in infectious diseases (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway analysis presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Mineral absorption was identified as a predominant pathway in KEGG analysis, with upregulation of Atp2b1, Atp7a, Mt2, Slc30a1, and Trpm7 genes.
source: Using KEGG pathway analysis, we identified mineral absorption as a predominant pathway, with upregulation of the Atp2b1, Atp7a, Mt2, Slc30a1, and Trpm7 genes.
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: Slc30a1 was ranked as the most significantly upregulated gene in human monocyte-derived macrophages infected with Salmonella.
source: Importantly, Slc30a1 was ranked as the most significantly upregulated gene and was therefore selected for further study.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data (GSE67427) from human macrophages.

claim: Slc30a1 expression peaked at 2 hr in Salmonella-treated BMDMs.
source: We found that Slc30a1 expression peaked at 2 and 4 hr in the Salmonella- and LPS-treated cells, respectively, while HK-ST produced a significantly smaller response that also peaked at 2 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Slc30a1 expression peaked at 4 hr in LPS-treated BMDMs.
source: We found that Slc30a1 expression peaked at 2 and 4 hr in the Salmonella- and LPS-treated cells, respectively, while HK-ST produced a significantly smaller response that also peaked at 2 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Heat-killed Salmonella typhimurium produced a significantly smaller Slc30a1 expression response that peaked at 2 hr.
source: We found that Slc30a1 expression peaked at 2 and 4 hr in the Salmonella- and LPS-treated cells, respectively, while HK-ST produced a significantly smaller response that also peaked at 2 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Slc30a1 expression was significantly higher in peritoneal macrophages at 4 hr post-infection compared to uninfected mice.
source: To validate this in vitro finding in vivo, we gave C57BL/6 mice an intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of a sublethal dose of attenuated Salmonella (1 × 105 CFU per mouse); at 4 hr post-infection (4 hpi), Slc30a1 expression was significantly higher in peritoneal macrophages compared to uninfected mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Salmonella-infected and ZnSO4-treated Slc30a1flag-EGFP/+ BMDMs had significantly higher levels of the reporter protein compared to untreated cells.
source: Compared to untreated WT and untreated Slc30a1flag-EGFP/+ BMDMs, both the Salmonella-infected and ZnSO4-treated Slc30a1flag-EGFP/+ BMDMs had significantly higher levels of the reporter protein (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ZnSO4 increased the levels of the Slc30a1-flag reporter, primarily in the plasma membrane.
source: As expected, we found that ZnSO4 increased the levels of the Slc30a1-flag reporter, primarily in the plasma membrane (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The Slc30a1-flag reporter was present both in the cytosol and in the plasma membrane in Salmonella-infected cells.
source: Interestingly, however, the Slc30a1-flag reporter was present both in the cytosol and in the plasma membrane in Salmonella-infected cells, suggesting that Slc30a1 may contribute to both zinc efflux and intracellular zinc movement in response to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Slc30a1 may contribute to both zinc efflux and intracellular zinc movement in response to Salmonella infection.
source: Interestingly, however, the Slc30a1-flag reporter was present both in the cytosol and in the plasma membrane in Salmonella-infected cells, suggesting that Slc30a1 may contribute to both zinc efflux and intracellular zinc movement in response to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Slc30a1 localization in both cytosol and plasma membrane.

claim: Slc30a1 is expressed at high levels specifically in splenic F4/80-positive cells at the area of red pulp in infected mice.
source: Immunostaining for Slc30a1-flag and the macrophage biomarker F4/80 revealed that Slc30a1 is expressed at high levels, specifically in splenic F4/80‒positive cells at the area of red pulp in infected mice, but not in uninfected mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Slc30a1 is not expressed at high levels in splenic F4/80-positive cells in uninfected mice.
source: Immunostaining for Slc30a1-flag and the macrophage biomarker F4/80 revealed that Slc30a1 is expressed at high levels, specifically in splenic F4/80‒positive cells at the area of red pulp in infected mice, but not in uninfected mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Salmonella-induced expression of Slc30a1 was confirmed by high GFP expression in CD11b+F4/80+ peritoneal macrophages.
source: Moreover, Salmonella-induced expression of Slc30a1 was confirmed by measuring high GFP expression in CD11b+F4/80+ peritoneal macrophages (Figure 3A) and splenic macrophages (Figure 3B, C), while there was no GFP expression in other splenic immune cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Salmonella-induced expression of Slc30a1 was confirmed by high GFP expression in splenic macrophages.
source: Moreover, Salmonella-induced expression of Slc30a1 was confirmed by measuring high GFP expression in CD11b+F4/80+ peritoneal macrophages (Figure 3A) and splenic macrophages (Figure 3B, C), while there was no GFP expression in other splenic immune cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: There was no GFP expression in other splenic immune cells following Salmonella infection.
source: Moreover, Salmonella-induced expression of Slc30a1 was confirmed by measuring high GFP expression in CD11b+F4/80+ peritoneal macrophages (Figure 3A) and splenic macrophages (Figure 3B, C), while there was no GFP expression in other splenic immune cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Slc30a1 expression was confirmed in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs, with a more than 95% reduction in Slc30a1 mRNA levels compared to Slc30a1fl/fl cells.
source: Loss of Slc30a1 expression was confirmed in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs, with a more than 95% reduction in Slc30a1 mRNA levels compared to Slc30a1fl/fl cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice had significantly lower survival compared to Salmonella-infected Slc30a1fl/fl mice.
source: We found that the Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice had significantly lower survival compared to Salmonella-infected Slc30a1fl/fl mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: At 24 hpi, severe tissue damage was observed in the spleen (deformation of white pulp tissue) and liver (necrotic tissue) of Slc30a1 cKO mice compared with Slc30a1fl/fl mice.
source: At 24 hpi, we observed severe tissue damage in the spleen (i.e., deformation of white pulp tissue) and liver (i.e., necrotic tissue) of Slc30a1 cKO mice when compared with Slc30a1fl/fl mice (Figure 4D, E)
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis presented in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice had higher levels of serum TNFα, ALT, and AST compared to Slc30a1fl/fl mice at 24 hpi.
source: as well as higher levels of serum TNFα, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) compared to Slc30a1fl/fl mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by serum measurements presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice contained a smaller proportion of CD11b+F4/80+ peritoneal macrophages compared to Salmonella-infected Slc30a1fl/fl mice.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice contained a smaller proportion of CD11b+F4/80+ peritoneal macrophages compared to Salmonella-infected Slc30a1fl/fl mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Significantly fewer neutrophils and monocytes were found in blood samples obtained at 24 hpi from infected Slc30a1 cKO mice compared to controls.
source: In addition, we found significantly fewer neutrophils and monocytes in blood samples obtained at 24 hpi from infected Slc30a1 cKO mice compared to controls without interruption of other blood parameters (Supplementary file 3), possibly due to the reported expression of Lyz2-Cre in neutrophils (Clausen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by blood cell count data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The reduction in neutrophils and monocytes in Slc30a1 cKO mice is possibly due to the reported expression of Lyz2-Cre in neutrophils.
source: In addition, we found significantly fewer neutrophils and monocytes in blood samples obtained at 24 hpi from infected Slc30a1 cKO mice compared to controls without interruption of other blood parameters (Supplementary file 3), possibly due to the reported expression of Lyz2-Cre in neutrophils (Clausen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the known expression pattern of Lyz2-Cre and supported by a citation.

claim: Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice had significantly higher numbers of bacterial cells in the peritoneal cavity, blood, spleen, and liver compared to control mice, particularly at 24 hpi.
source: We also quantified Salmonella burden at 4, 24, and 48 hpi and found significantly higher numbers of bacterial cells in the peritoneal cavity, blood, spleen, and liver of infected Slc30a1 cKO mice compared to control mice, particularly at 24 hpi (Figure 4G), indicating severe systemic infection.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial burden measurements presented in Figure 4G.

claim: The higher bacterial burden in Slc30a1 cKO mice indicates severe systemic infection.
source: We also quantified Salmonella burden at 4, 24, and 48 hpi and found significantly higher numbers of bacterial cells in the peritoneal cavity, blood, spleen, and liver of infected Slc30a1 cKO mice compared to control mice, particularly at 24 hpi (Figure 4G), indicating severe systemic infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of high bacterial burden across multiple organs.

claim: Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs contained a significantly higher intracellular bacterial load compared to control cells at both 8 and 24 hr.
source: We found that Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs contained a significantly higher intracellular bacterial load compared to control cells at both 8 and 24 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial killing assay data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy revealed increased numbers of bacterial cells in the phagosomes of Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs at 24 hr compared to control cells.
source: Moreover, examining the cells at high magnification using transmission electron microscopy revealed increased numbers of bacterial cells in the phagosomes of Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs at 24 hr compared to control cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy images presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Infected Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs showed significantly reduced expression of proinflammatory cytokine- and chemokine-related genes compared to control cells.
source: We found significantly reduced expression of proinflammatory cytokine- and chemokine-related genes in infected Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs compared to control cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data for cytokines and chemokines presented in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Extremely low levels of Nos2 mRNA were found in infected Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs.
source: In particular, we found extremely low levels of Nos2 mRNA in infected Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs; Nos2 encodes iNOS, a hallmark of classically activated macrophages that contributes to the host defense system by producing NO.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Nos2 encodes iNOS, a hallmark of classically activated macrophages that contributes to the host defense system by producing NO.
source: In particular, we found extremely low levels of Nos2 mRNA in infected Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs; Nos2 encodes iNOS, a hallmark of classically activated macrophages that contributes to the host defense system by producing NO.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Nos2/iNOS.

claim: Downregulation of the Nos2 gene was supported by low levels of iNOS protein in Salmonella-infected BMDMs.
source: Downregulation of the Nos2 gene was supported by the low levels of iNOS (Figure 5F—source data 1) and nitrite concentrations (Figure 5G) in Salmonella-infected BMDMs.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Downregulation of the Nos2 gene was supported by low nitrite concentrations in Salmonella-infected BMDMs.
source: Downregulation of the Nos2 gene was supported by the low levels of iNOS (Figure 5F—source data 1) and nitrite concentrations (Figure 5G) in Salmonella-infected BMDMs.
evidence: This is supported by nitrite concentration measurements presented in Figure 5G.

claim: Reduced expression of Nos2 and proinflammatory cytokine-related genes was found in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs exposed to HK-ST or LPS compared to control cells.
source: In addition, we found reduced expression of Nos2 and a number of proinflammatory cytokine-related genes in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs exposed to either HK-ST or LPS compared to control cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed that both HK-ST and LPS downregulate Nos2 in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs compared to control cells.
source: Western blot analysis of iNOS protein levels confirmed that both HK-ST and LPS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D, Figure 5—source data 2) downregulate Nos2 in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs compared to control cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: Significantly lower levels of nitrite were measured in the cell culture supernatant of Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs 24 hr after HK-ST and LPS compared to control cells.
source: Moreover, we measured significantly lower levels of nitrite (NO2−), a product of NO metabolism, in the cell culture supernatant of Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs 24 hr after HK-ST and LPS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) compared to control cells.
evidence: This is supported by nitrite measurements presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: p-p65 levels were significantly lower in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs at 60 min after LPS stimulation.
source: Western blot analysis revealed that p-p65, p-Erk, p-p38, and p-Stat3 levels were raised within 30 min in both Slc30a1 cKO and Slc30a1fl/fl BMDMs; however, p-p65 levels were significantly lower in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs at 60 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Salmonella infection caused lower levels of p-p65 protein in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs at 60 min compared to infected Slc30a1fl/fl cells.
source: Similarly, Salmonella infection (MOI = 1) caused lower levels of p-p65 protein in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs at 60 min compared to infected Slc30a1fl/fl cells (Figure 5H—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 5H.

claim: Salmonella infection caused reduced mRNA levels of p65, MyD88, Ikkα, and Ikkβ in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs.
source: as well as reduced mRNA levels of several genes upstream of the NF-κB pathway, including p65, MyD88, Ikkα, and Ikkβ (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 5I.

claim: Salmonella-induced changes in the expression of key NF-κB signaling molecules were prevented by treating cells with TPEN.
source: Notably, these Salmonella-induced changes in the expression of these key NF-κB signaling molecules were prevented by treating cells with the membrane-permeable zinc chelator TPEN (N, N,N′,N′-tetrakis-(2-pyridyl-methyl)-ethylenediamine (TPEN)) (Figure 5J—source data 1, Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 5J and 5K.

claim: Slc30a1 in macrophages protects against Salmonella infection by regulating intracellular zinc.
source: These results suggest that Slc30a1 in macrophages protects against Salmonella infection by regulating intracellular zinc.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TPEN treatment rescues NF-κB signaling defects in Slc30a1-deficient cells.

claim: Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice had significantly higher levels of zinc in the serum and spleen but no difference in the liver compared to control mice.
source: We found that compared to Salmonella-infected control mice, Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice had significantly higher levels of zinc in the serum and spleen but no difference in the liver (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by ICP-MS measurements presented in Figure 6A.

claim: During systemic infection, serum zinc is redistributed to the liver to increase monocyte maturation, boost the immune system, and restrict the delivery of nutrient metals to pathogens.
source: consistent with the previous finding that during systemic infection serum zinc is redistributed to the liver in order to increase monocyte maturation, boost the immune system, and restrict the delivery of nutrient metals to pathogens (Alker and Haase, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alker and Haase, 2018.

claim: Elevated serum zinc may impair the function of immune cells, leading to increased susceptibility to Salmonella infection.
source: In addition, elevated serum zinc may impair the function of immune cells, leading to increased susceptibility to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of elevated serum zinc in susceptible Slc30a1 cKO mice.

claim: The spleen serves to filter the blood and is a hub for monocytes.
source: Moreover, the spleen serves to filter the blood filter and is a hub for monocytes (Swirski et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Swirski et al., 2009.

claim: The high zinc content in the spleen may be due to circulating high zinc-containing macrophages.
source: thus, the high zinc content in the spleen may be due to circulating high zinc‒containing macrophages, a notion supported by our finding of increased mRNA levels of Mt1, which encodes the principal splenic zinc reservoir protein metallothionein 1, in the spleen of Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice, but not in the liver (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of high splenic zinc and increased Mt1 expression.

claim: Increased mRNA levels of Mt1 were found in the spleen of Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice, but not in the liver.
source: thus, the high zinc content in the spleen may be due to circulating high zinc‒containing macrophages, a notion supported by our finding of increased mRNA levels of Mt1, which encodes the principal splenic zinc reservoir protein metallothionein 1, in the spleen of Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice, but not in the liver (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Mt1 encodes the principal splenic zinc reservoir protein metallothionein 1.
source: thus, the high zinc content in the spleen may be due to circulating high zinc‒containing macrophages, a notion supported by our finding of increased mRNA levels of Mt1, which encodes the principal splenic zinc reservoir protein metallothionein 1, in the spleen of Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO mice, but not in the liver (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Mt1.

claim: Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs were significantly more sensitive to ZnSO4-induced toxicity compared to control cells.
source: Consistent with the well-documented role of Slc30a1 in zinc resistance (Palmiter, 2004), we found that Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs were significantly more sensitive to ZnSO4-induced toxicity compared to control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ZnSO4 treatment caused a significantly higher FluoZin-3 signal in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs compared to control cells.
source: and ZnSO4 treatment (100 µM) caused a significantly higher FluoZin-3 signal in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs compared to control cells (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is supported by FluoZin-3 fluorescence measurements presented in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Cytosolic-free zinc increases in macrophages following exposure to LPS, Escherichia coli, and Salmonella.
source: Previous studies showed that cytosolic-free zinc increases in macrophages following exposure to LPS, Escherichia coli, and Salmonella (Haase et al., 2008; Brieger et al., 2013, Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haase et al., 2008; Brieger et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017.

claim: 30 min after Salmonella infection, FluoZin-3 fluorescence was significantly higher in Slc30a1 cKO cells compared to control cells.
source: We, therefore, measured intracellular free zinc in Salmonella-infected Slc30a1 cKO and control BMDMs. We found that 30 min after Salmonella infection (MOI = 1), FluoZin-3 fluorescence was significantly higher in Slc30a1 cKO cells; similar results were obtained when the cells were exposed to H2O2 (1 mM), LPS (1 µg/ml), or HK-ST (MOI = 100) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by FluoZin-3 fluorescence measurements presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Higher levels of Mt1 mRNA were measured in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs compared to Slc30a1fl/fl cells, even in uninfected cells.
source: In addition, we measured higher levels of Mt1 mRNA in Slc30a1 cKO BMDMs compared to Slc30a1fl/fl cells, even in uninfected cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: The loss of Slc30a1 leads to an abnormal increase in intracellular zinc during Salmonella infection and increases the expression of Mt1, possibly to compensate for the excessive intracellular zinc by increasing Mt1-mediated zinc storage.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesize that the loss of Slc30a1 leads to an abnormal increase in intracellular zinc during Salmonella infection and increases the expression of Mt1, possibly to compensate for the excessive intracellular zinc by increasing Mt1-mediated zinc storage (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the combined observations of zinc accumulation and Mt1 upregulation.

claim: Slc30a1-deficient macrophages have increased Salmonella burden due to reduced iNOS and NO formation via reduced NF-κB signaling.
source: Based on this model, Slc30a1-deficient macrophages have increased Salmonella burden due to reduced iNOS and NO formation via reduced NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of Slc30a1 deficiency on bacterial burden is due primarily to the inhibitory effects of high intracellular zinc, reflected by the compensatory upregulation of the zinc-binding protein Mt1.
source: This effect is due primarily to the inhibitory effects of high intracellular zinc, reflected by the compensatory upregulation of the zinc-binding protein Mt1.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of zinc accumulation, Mt1 upregulation, and impaired bacterial killing.

claim: Slc30a1 in macrophages mediates the intracellular killing of invading Mycobacterium tuberculosis and E. coli by increasing zinc levels within phagosomes.
source: Previous in vitro studies have shown that Slc30a1 in macrophages mediates the intracellular killing of invading Mycobacterium tuberculosis and E. coli by increasing zinc levels within phagosomes, thereby promoting bacterial clearance (Botella et al., 2011; Stocks et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Botella et al., 2011 and Stocks et al., 2021.

claim: This study provides the first in vivo evidence that Slc30a1 in macrophages plays a key role in host protection against Salmonella infection.
source: Here, we provide the first in vivo evidence that Slc30a1 in macrophages plays a key role in host protection against Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mice lacking Slc30a1 in macrophages are highly susceptible to Salmonella infection.
source: We show that mice lacking Slc30a1 in macrophages are highly susceptible to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is supported by survival and bacterial burden data from the conditional knockout mice.

claim: Macrophages isolated from Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice have reduced pathogen-killing capacity via reduced NF-κB signaling, decreasing iNOS and NO production.
source: Using BMDMs isolated from our Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice, we show that these macrophages have reduced pathogen-killing capacity via reduced NF-κB signaling, decreasing iNOS and NO production.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial killing assays and measurements of NF-κB signaling and NO production.

claim: Treating Slc30a1-deficient macrophages with the zinc chelator TPEN improves NF-κB signaling.
source: Interestingly, we found that treating these cells with the zinc chelator TPEN improves NF-κB signaling, suggesting that changes in cellular zinc levels likely contribute to their reduced antimicrobial function.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and RT-qPCR data showing rescue of NF-κB signaling with TPEN treatment.

claim: Changes in cellular zinc levels likely contribute to the reduced antimicrobial function of Slc30a1-deficient macrophages.
source: Interestingly, we found that treating these cells with the zinc chelator TPEN improves NF-κB signaling, suggesting that changes in cellular zinc levels likely contribute to their reduced antimicrobial function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TPEN treatment rescues NF-κB signaling defects.

claim: Zinc can suppress iNOS/NO production by inhibiting NF-κB in Salmonella-infected macrophages.
source: Wu et al. previously reported that zinc can suppress iNOS/NO production by inhibiting NF-κB in Salmonella-infected macrophages (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Zinc can reduce NF-κB activation in macrophages.
source: Moreover, recent studies have shown that zinc can reduce NF-κB activation in macrophages (Haase et al., 2008; Brieger et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017; Jeon et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haase et al., 2008; Brieger et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017; Jeon et al., 2000.

claim: Zinc inhibits the NF-κB pathway by reducing the activity of recombinant IKKα and IKKβ by blocking IκBα phosphorylation and degradation.
source: With respect to the underlying mechanism, studies have shown that zinc inhibits the NF-κB pathway by reducing the activity of recombinant IKKα and IKKβ by blocking IκBα phosphorylation and degradation (Jeon et al., 2000; Zhou et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeon et al., 2000; Zhou et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice fail to redistribute zinc levels in the serum and spleen following Salmonella infection.
source: An interesting finding from our in vivo experiments is that our Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice fail to redistribute zinc levels in the serum and spleen following Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is supported by ICP-MS measurements of zinc in serum and spleen.

claim: Defects in zinc redistribution to the liver during systemic infection have negative consequences for neutrophil extracellular traps in mice.
source: In mice, defects in this process—for example, due to high zinc supplementation—have negative consequences for neutrophil extracellular traps (Kuźmicka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuźmicka et al., 2020.

claim: In infants, consuming a full-fat diet of powdered cow's milk containing excessive zinc content can lead to a decreased phagocytic capacity of monocytes.
source: In infants, consuming a full-fat diet of powdered cow's milk containing excessive zinc content can lead to a decreased phagocytic capacity of monocytes (Schlesinger et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schlesinger et al., 1993.

claim: In adults, excessive consumption of zinc supplements can impair both the migration and bactericidal capacity of polymorphonuclear leukocytes.
source: In adults, excessive consumption of zinc supplements can impair both the migration and bactericidal capacity of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (Chandra, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chandra, 1984.

claim: High zinc serum level in Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice affects the percentage of neutrophils and monocytes and the migration of macrophages, thereby reducing bacterial clearance and increasing susceptibility to Salmonella infection.
source: This is consistent with our finding that a high zinc serum level in our Lyz2-Cre-driven Slc30a1 conditional knockout mice affects the percentage of neutrophils and monocytes and the migration of macrophages, thereby reducing bacterial clearance and increasing their susceptibility to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of high serum zinc, reduced immune cell numbers, and increased susceptibility to infection.

claim: Nutrient-dense conditions such as excessive serum zinc can be beneficial to the growth of Salmonella.
source: Furthermore, nutrient-dense conditions such as excessive serum zinc can be beneficial to the growth of Salmonella.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial growth under nutrient-rich conditions.

claim: A high-affinity Zn2+ uptake system ZnuABC of Salmonella protects the bacterial cells from nitrosative stress in macrophages.
source: Previous studies reported that a high-affinity Zn2+ uptake system ZnuABC of Salmonella protects the bacterial cells from nitrosative stress in macrophages (Fitzsimmons et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fitzsimmons et al., 2018.

claim: Zinc rich conditions induce peptide deformylase, an essential protein contributing to Salmonella maturation that can be inhibited by NO.
source: Zinc rich also induces peptide deformylase, an essential protein contributing to Salmonella maturation that can be inhibited by NO (Singhal and Fang, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Singhal and Fang, 2020.

claim: High zinc concentrations were measured in Slc30a1-deficient macrophages.
source: Our measurements of intracellular zinc levels revealed high zinc concentrations in Slc30a1-deficient macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by FluoZin-3 fluorescence measurements.

claim: An upregulation of Mt1 was detected in Slc30a1-deficient macrophages, possibly indicating a cellular response to intracellular zinc saturation.
source: We also detected an upregulation of Mt1, possibly indicating a cellular response to intracellular zinc saturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Mt1 upregulation in cells with high intracellular zinc.

claim: Mt1 is a low molecular weight cysteine-rich protein with a high affinity for divalent metals that is essential for buffering surplus zinc to maintain zinc homeostasis.
source: Mt1 is a low molecular weight cysteine-rich protein with a high affinity for divalent metals that is essential for buffering surplus zinc to maintain zinc homeostasis (Krężel and Maret, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krężel and Maret, 2017.

claim: The level of Mt1 expression was positively correlated with intracellular free zinc concentration.
source: Smith et al. showed that the level of Mt1 expression was positively correlated with intracellular free zinc concentration (Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2008.

claim: Mt1 overexpression may serve as zinc storage for reducing the side effects of excessive cytosolic-free zinc due to Slc30a1 deletion.
source: In this respect, Mt1 overexpression may serve as zinc storage for reducing the side effects of excessive cytosolic-free zinc due to Slc30a1 deletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Mt1 upregulation in Slc30a1-deficient cells with high intracellular zinc.

claim: Slc30a1 in macrophages plays a protective role against Salmonella infection by regulating iNOS and NO activities, which are essential for bacterial clearance through NF-κB signaling.
source: In conclusion, we report that Slc30a1 of macrophages plays a protective role against Salmonella infection by regulating iNOS and NO activities, which are essential for bacterial clearance through NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusions of the study.

claim: Cellular zinc regulated by zinc transporter Slc30a1 is important for host defenses by maintaining an intracellular killing capacity of macrophages.
source: These findings underscore the notion that cellular zinc regulated by zinc transporter Slc30a1 is important for host defenses by maintaining an intracellular killing capacity of macrophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined findings of the study.
